intro: Baltimore's oldest tree is a white oak that predates the city itself by more than a century, a survivor of the colonial landscape still growing over a suburban road on private land its owners keep alive with weekly deep watering. Two more stand near downtown: a Camden Yards elm local tradition says Frederick Douglass planted as an enslaved boy, and two record-holding specimens in the city's own Cylburn Arboretum, a hawthorn armed with finger-length thorns and a maple that sheds its bark in cinnamon curls.
meta_description: Baltimore's trees: a 17th-century oak that predates the city, an elm tradition ties to Frederick Douglass, and two record specimens at Cylburn Arboretum.
question_meta: Baltimore's oldest tree is the Ruxton Liberty Tree, a white oak roughly 350 to 380 years old, growing over Bellona Avenue.
question_answer: Baltimore's oldest tree is the Ruxton Liberty Tree, a white oak in the Ruxton neighbourhood of Baltimore County estimated at 350 to 380 years old, meaning it was already a seedling around 1646, twelve years after the first English colonists landed in Maryland. It stands on private land at the corner of Dunlora Road and Bellona Avenue, and the family who own the lawn spend 5,000 gallons of water a week keeping it alive.
question_context: The Ruxton Liberty Tree's age comes from a documented use as a surveyor's boundary marker in 1694, which means it was already substantial enough to serve that role only 48 years after the first English colonists reached Maryland, and from the girth of its trunk today, 5.49 metres round under a canopy roughly 150 feet across. Keeping it alive costs real money and effort: the family who own the lawn it grows on pay for 5,000 gallons of water a week and for fungicide treatments against a root disease working at its base. Baltimore's other old trees are younger and thinner on the record. The Frederick Douglass Elm near Camden Yards carries no documented age at all, only a local tradition that Douglass planted it as a child while enslaved in the city and returned to speak beneath it in 1878 as a free man, alongside TreeBaltimore's own listing of it as a notable specimen. Two more, a state-champion hawthorn and a city-champion paperbark maple, grow in the city's own Cylburn Arboretum; neither has a published age, since Maryland's champion registers measure trunk size and crown spread rather than years.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Baltimore?
faq.a: The Ruxton Liberty Tree, a white oak in Baltimore County estimated at 350 to 380 years old. It grows on private land over Bellona Avenue, and the family who own the property keep it alive with weekly deep watering and fungicide treatment.

faq.q: Did Frederick Douglass really plant a tree in Baltimore?
faq.a: No document proves it. Local tradition holds that Douglass planted the English elm near Camden Yards as a boy, while enslaved in the city, and that he returned to speak beneath it in 1878 as a free man. We keep the story in the honest form it is told in, as tradition rather than fact.

faq.q: Are Baltimore's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Cylburn Arboretum, home to the hawthorn and the paperbark maple, is a free public arboretum open daily except Mondays. The Frederick Douglass Elm stands in a public park near Camden Yards. The Ruxton Liberty Tree is on private land, visible from the road at Dunlora Road and Bellona Avenue.

A 207-acre city-owned arboretum in northwest Baltimore, free to enter, holding Baltimore's cockspur hawthorn, once described as its last remaining state champion tree, and a city-champion paperbark maple known for its cinnamon-coloured, peeling bark.

trees.name: The Ruxton Liberty Tree

location.address: Intersection of Dunlora Road and Bellona Avenue, Ruxton, facing St. John's AME Church

trees.access: The tree stands on PRIVATE PROPERTY (owned by the Anastasiades family) but is directly beside and clearly visible from the public roadway (Bellona Avenue), which motorists and pedestrians pass under its canopy on every day. Visitors can view and photograph it from the road; there is no suggestion anyone may step onto the private lawn itself. State plainly: viewable from the road, not enterable.
trees.transport: Ruxton, a suburb about 11km/7 miles north of downtown Baltimore; nearest Baltimore Light Rail stop is Falls Road, roughly 2km/a 25-minute walk away, otherwise a roughly 20-25 minute drive from downtown.
trees.story:
Keeping this oak alive takes 5,000 gallons of water a week. The family who own the lawn it grows on pay for that, and for the fungicide treatments against the phytophthora working at its roots, because the tree leaning over Bellona Avenue was a seedling around 1646, twelve years after the first English colonists landed in Maryland.

By 1694 it was big enough to be useful. Surveyors used it to mark the boundary between two land grants, Young Man's Adventure and Samuel Hope, in the same year Maryland moved its government from St Mary's City to Annapolis. It outlasted the Bellona Gunpowder Works, which supplied ammunition for the War of 1812 nearby, and it was already close to two centuries old when the Baltimore and Susquehanna Railroad came through in the 1830s. Local legend has Abraham Lincoln catching sight of it from a train in 1863. Nobody has ever sourced that, and it is repeated here as legend rather than fact.

The Baltimore Sun measured it in 2002 at over 100 feet tall, with a canopy spanning roughly 150 feet and a trunk 18 feet around. A more recent account of the man who cares for it calls it nearly 400 years old and describes the watering still going on.

It grows on private ground. Stand on the road beneath the branches and look up, which is as far as anyone should go.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.49 metres round, under a canopy roughly 150 feet across that reaches out over the road. It stands at the corner of Dunlora Road and Bellona Avenue, facing St John's AME Church.
trees.why_go: A white oak that was already generations old when Lincoln's train may have passed it in 1863, marking a property line drawn in 1694, still growing over Bellona Avenue on private land its owners keep alive with weekly deep watering.

trees.name: The Frederick Douglass Elm

location.address: Intersection of West Hill Street and Sharp Street, Hermitage Park, Otterbein

verified_sources: search-corroborated citation of https://darkroom.baltimoresun.com/2017/06/baltimores-big-trees/ (page returned HTTP 500 on direct fetch this pass; its specific wording -- 'the orator addressed Baltimoreans beneath the same limbs, in 1878', location and species -- was corroborated identically across three independent search queries, but was not read on the page itself; treat as thin until a future pass can fetch it directly)
trees.access: Free. Public property at a city street intersection in Otterbein, near Oriole Park at Camden Yards.
trees.transport: Downtown Baltimore, Otterbein neighbourhood, walkable from Camden Yards and the Inner Harbor (about 10-15 minutes).
trees.story:
Baltimore tradition holds that Frederick Douglass planted this elm as a boy, while he was still enslaved in the city. No document proves it. The people who pass the story on say some believe it, which is the honest form of the claim and the form we are keeping.

What is on the record is thinner and more solid: TreeBaltimore, the city's own forestry programme, lists this English elm among Baltimore's notable trees, standing where West Hill Street meets Sharp Street in Otterbein, a short walk from Camden Yards. By the same local memory, Douglass came back to it. An account repeated around the city, which we have not managed to read at its original source, says he addressed a Baltimore crowd beneath these limbs in 1878, forty years after he escaped slavery from this city and went north. Treat the return as story rather than record until somebody produces the page.

The species is its own piece of history. English elms went into American cities by the thousand in the nineteenth century, and Dutch elm disease took most of them from the 1930s onward, which is why a mature one on a street corner now stops people who know what they are looking at. Neighbours have reported bigger branches coming down in recent years.

Nobody has dated it and nobody has put a tape around it. If you know either number, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the elm on the corner, a species Dutch elm disease made rare on American streets. It stands where West Hill Street meets Sharp Street, at Hermitage Park in Otterbein, minutes from Camden Yards.
trees.why_go: An English elm a Baltimore tradition says Frederick Douglass planted as an enslaved child, and where local memory holds he returned in 1878 to speak beneath its limbs as a free man; still standing minutes from Camden Yards.

trees.name: The Cockspur Hawthorn of Cylburn Arboretum

location.address: Cylburn Arboretum, 4915 Greenspring Ave, Baltimore, MD 21209 (exact spot within the 207-acre grounds not pinned this pass; not one of the 17 specimens on the arboretum's own printed 'Notable Trees' map, so it stands somewhere else on the property)

verified_sources: https://www.baltimoresun.com/2023/11/29/touring-baltimores-big-trees-in-an-oasis-of-beauty-guest-commentary/ (Baltimore Sun guest commentary, 29 Nov 2023, by a named tree tour guide describing a walk through Cylburn Arboretum: calls this tree 'Cylburn's only remaining state champion' and describes it firsthand in late autumn as 'leafless but teeming with berry-like fruit called haws', with 'long sharp thorns that resemble a giant's toothpick' -- a specific, physically checkable eyewitness description, not a copied stat)
trees.access: Free, public city-owned arboretum (Baltimore City Department of Recreation and Parks / Cylburn Arboretum Friends). Open daily except Mondays, no admission charge, per Wikipedia's Cylburn Arboretum article and the arboretum's own trail map.
trees.transport: Northwest Baltimore, accessible by MTA Bus Route #1; parking on site.
trees.verify_notes: SINGLE SOURCE this pass, shipped per Step 2's explicit rule that a single-sourced tree ships flagged rather than being held back. Tried and failed to get a second source or exact location in the time available: (1) Cylburn Arboretum Friends' own official 'Notable Trees' map (cylburn.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/cylburn_tree_shrubs_map.pdf), which letter-codes 17 specimens A-Q with approximate positions relative to the Mansion/Visitor Center/Greenhouses, does NOT include this hawthorn -- it lists a Castor Aralia (Kalopanax pictus) as the arboretum's STATE Champion (point O on that map) instead, which conflicts with the Sun's 2023 'only remaining state champion' description of the hawthorn. Read together, the two most likely explanations are that the printed map (undated on its face, hosted since at least 2013) is simply older than 2023 and the Castor Aralia has since died or lost its state-champion status, or that the map was never a complete list of every champion on the grounds. Either way, DO NOT independently repeat the Castor Aralia's 'State Champion' label as current fact without rechecking it (left as a separate lead below). (2) The Maryland Big Tree Program's own database (mdbigtrees.org, 'Tree Listings'/'State Champion Trees') is JS-rendered and would not return tree-level data to this pass's fetch tool; a future pass with a JS-capable fetch or the ability to query its underlying data could likely get exact circumference/height/crown and possibly a precise location, which would let this tree's location_precision move from approximate to confirmed. (3) TreeBaltimore's own notable-trees page mentions an interactive ArcGIS 'Notable Tree Map' for the whole city but the page fetched did not surface a Cylburn/hawthorn entry directly; the ArcGIS web app itself (arcgis.com webappviewer id d2cfbbe9a24b4d988de127852e6c26c8) was not queryable with the tools available this pass. No girth or height figure was found anywhere this pass; the Sun's description is purely visual/seasonal (bare branches, red haws, long thorns), which is itself decent 'alive and observed recently' evidence (Nov 2023) even without measurements. location_precision is approximate at the arboretum's own address/coordinate, honestly short of pinning which part of the 207-acre grounds holds it.
trees.story:
Cylburn Arboretum's cockspur hawthorn carries thorns long enough that a Baltimore Sun guest columnist compared them to a giant's toothpick, straight, sharp and several inches each, the kind farmers once grew into living fences because nothing could push through them. This one grows loose rather than clipped, somewhere in the arboretum's 207 acres on Baltimore's northwest side.

The same columnist, touring the grounds in late 2023, called it Cylburn's only remaining state champion, the last of a run of record trees the arboretum used to hold more of. That claim sits next to a complication: the arboretum's own printed trail map names a different tree, a castor aralia, as the state champion instead. Titles like this move when a tree grows, dies or gets remeasured, and a printed map does not always catch up. Either the aralia has since lost the title or the map is simply the older document.

What the newspaper account gives that the map cannot is a direct look, taken in November: bare branches carrying a heavy load of small red haws, and those thorns.

Nobody has measured its girth or dated it, and this pass could not pin which part of the grounds it stands on. If you find it, the thorns and the fruit are how you will know.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thorns, several inches long and straight, and by the small red haws that hang on through a leafless November. It stands somewhere in the arboretum grounds; nobody has pinned the exact spot.
trees.why_go: A hawthorn a Baltimore Sun tour guide called Cylburn Arboretum's last remaining state champion, armed with thorns long enough to compare to a giant's toothpick.

trees.name: The Paperbark Maple of Cylburn Arboretum

location.address: Cylburn Arboretum, 4915 Greenspring Ave, Baltimore, MD 21209, near the Visitor Center (marked point 'A' on the arboretum's own printed trail map, close to the parking area and Greenspring Ave entrance)

verified_sources: https://www.baltimoresun.com/2023/11/29/touring-baltimores-big-trees-in-an-oasis-of-beauty-guest-commentary/ (Baltimore Sun guest commentary, 29 Nov 2023: names this a Baltimore City Champion, gives a champion score of 91 points, and describes it firsthand: 'exfoliating and intense cinnamon colored bark')

https://cylburn.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/cylburn_tree_shrubs_map.pdf (Cylburn Arboretum Friends' own official 'Notable Trees' map: point A, 'Paperbark Maple, Acer griseum, City Champion', positioned just southeast of the Visitor Center near the Greenspring Ave entrance -- an independent institutional source, not the newspaper, naming and mapping the same tree with the same champion designation)
trees.access: Free, public city-owned arboretum (Baltimore City Department of Recreation and Parks / Cylburn Arboretum Friends). Open daily except Mondays, no admission charge.
trees.transport: Northwest Baltimore, accessible by MTA Bus Route #1; on-site parking near the Visitor Center, a short walk from point A on the arboretum's own map.
trees.verify_notes: Two independent sources agree on species and City Champion status: the Sun's 2023 firsthand description (bark colour, champion score of 91 points -- the American Forests index, trunk circumference in inches + height in feet + 1/4 average crown spread in feet, not a measurement in itself) and Cylburn Arboretum Friends' own trail map, which places it at labelled point A near the Visitor Center. No circumference, height or age figure found directly (the 91-point score cannot be reverse-engineered into any one of those three without the others, so it is not decomposed here to avoid inventing a number). Paperbark maple is a slow-growing, small ornamental species prized for its exfoliating cinnamon-coloured bark, which is the visible, checkable feature both sources independently point to. location_precision is approximate: point A on the arboretum's own map gives a specific corner of the grounds (near the Visitor Center/parking, by the Greenspring Ave entrance) rather than the full 207 acres, which is a real improvement over park-level, but this pass did not get a GPS-grade coordinate, so it is not marked confirmed. A future pass with a JS-capable fetch against the Maryland Big Tree Program's own database (mdbigtrees.org) may be able to get exact measurements and a precise coordinate for this and the hawthorn above.
trees.story:
A paperbark maple sheds its own bark in curls of cinnamon and copper, thin as paper, and it keeps doing that in every season, which is the whole reason anyone plants one where people will walk past it in winter. Cylburn Arboretum's specimen stands a few steps from the Visitor Center, close enough to the Greenspring Avenue entrance that most visits pass within sight of it without meaning to.

The arboretum's own trail map marks the spot as point A and names it a City Champion. A Baltimore Sun guest columnist, touring the grounds in November 2023, gave it a champion score of 91 points and singled out the same feature the map cannot show: bark peeling back in bright, exfoliating strips. An institution and a firsthand account, written months apart, naming the same tree at the same corner of the grounds.

Neither source gives a single number. A champion score is calculated from circumference, height and crown spread together, and pulling one figure back out of the total would mean inventing what nobody measured directly, so this page carries none. Paperbark maple is naturally a slow, small tree, and holding the city title here says more about how rare the species still is in Baltimore than about size.

Go in low winter light, when the bark catches it best.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark: thin curls of cinnamon and copper peeling back in every season, not just autumn. It stands a few steps from the Visitor Center, near the Greenspring Avenue entrance.
trees.why_go: Baltimore's champion paperbark maple, its cinnamon bark peeling in curls year round, a short walk from the arboretum entrance.
